title: University students who live rent-free in homes for older people (Humanitas Deventer, the Netherlands) and similar programs in Sydney and Michigan

facts.text: At the Humanitas home for older people in Deventer, the Netherlands, university students live in small apartments without paying rent.
In return, each student spends at least 30 hours a month acting as a good neighbor to the residents.
The students are in their early twenties, and most residents are in their eighties and nineties.
Six students from two local universities, Saxion and Windesheim, shared the building with about 160 older residents.
The idea came from a student who complained to the head of the home, Gea Sijpkes, about noise and poor conditions in student housing; their talks led to the exchange.
Students may come and go as they like, as long as they do not become a nuisance to the older residents.
The head of the home has described the students as good neighbors, not caregivers.
The students watch sports with residents, celebrate birthdays with them and keep them company when they are ill.
Students have taught residents to use email, social media and video calls, and even graffiti art.
The program is based on research showing that reducing loneliness and social isolation improves older people's well-being and helps them live longer.
About 1 in 6 people worldwide are affected by loneliness, and social isolation may affect up to 1 in 3 older adults.
Loneliness is linked to an estimated 871,000 deaths a year, about 100 every hour, and raises the risk of stroke, heart disease and depression.
In 2018 a nursing home in southern Sydney began giving four health students from the University of Sydney free rooms and meals for 30 hours of company a month.
The Sydney students have no fixed list of tasks; the lack of structure is deliberate, so that visits happen naturally, such as listening to music or going out for coffee.
Staff in the Sydney home noted that nurses look after residents' health but often cannot stop for a long chat, which the students can offer.
From August 2016 to April 2018, three graduate students from Western Michigan University lived in a retirement community near Grand Rapids with about 40 older residents.
The Michigan students lived there full time, paid no housing costs, and were encouraged to spend at least 30 hours a month with their neighbors; the idea was inspired by the Dutch program.
Some Michigan residents were slow to open up; living into their eighties and nineties had meant losing many friends, and they were reluctant to start new friendships they might soon lose too.
While the Michigan students lived there, 15 residents died, including several people the students considered friends.
The Michigan students said living with older people gave them insights they could not easily have gained any other way.
A 2017 U.S. survey found that 61 percent of adults aged 18 to 34 knew few people who were much older or much younger than themselves.
